definition.text: A predator at the top of a food chain that has few or no natural predators of its own.

facts.text: Apex predators occupy the highest trophic levels; on land chains are shorter, so wolves mostly eat large herbivores that eat plants.
They are central to how ecosystems function, to regulating disease and to maintaining biodiversity.
Predators that exert top-down control are often considered keystone species.
After gray wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995, elk declined and changed behaviour, letting willows, aspens and cottonwoods flourish and creating habitat for beavers and moose.
Humans have hunted many apex predators close to extinction, and climate change now threatens species such as the polar bear by shrinking Arctic sea ice.
Ecotourism sometimes relies on apex predators, and rewilding efforts have reintroduced species such as the Iberian lynx.
Reintroducing large predators is controversial, partly because farmers fear for their livestock.

definition.text: The rise in mid-sized predators that follows when the top predators that kept them in check are removed.

facts.text: Hunting of sperm whales, with a trophic level of 4.7, has increased populations of large squid.
In North America over the past two centuries, the ranges of all apex carnivores have shrunk while those of 60% of mesopredators have grown.
Removing badgers in a bovine tuberculosis trial more than doubled hedgehog densities.

title: Human trophic level

definition.text: The question of where humans sit in the food web, and whether they count as apex predators.

facts.text: A 2013 study averaged the trophic levels of foods in the human diet and found a mean of 2.21, from 2.04 in Burundi to 2.57 in Iceland.
That value is comparable to non-apex animals such as the anchovy or pig.
A 2014 critique found humans eating mainly predatory fish in two marine systems had trophic levels of 4.65 and 4.5, making them apex predators there.

contested_note: Ecologists disagree whether humans are apex predators, depending on whether land-based diets or marine food webs are measured.

definition.text: An organism that turns non-living energy sources, such as sunlight or chemicals, into energy stored in organic compounds that others can use.

facts.text: Autotrophs build carbohydrates, fats and proteins from carbon in simple substances such as carbon dioxide.
They are the producers in a food chain, such as plants on land and algae in water, and need no living source of carbon or energy.
Heterotrophs, including all animals and almost all fungi, depend on autotrophs for raw materials and fuel.
Plants can use only about 1% of the sun's energy for photosynthesis.
The German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank coined the term in 1892.
Researchers think the first cells were autotrophs, possibly living at deep-sea hydrothermal vents.

definition.text: An organism that makes its food using energy from chemical reactions of inorganic substances instead of light.

facts.text: They are often found at deep-ocean hydrothermal vents and include some archaea and bacteria.
They use substances such as hydrogen, iron, nitrogen and sulfur to generate energy.
In deep-sea vent ecosystems without sunlight, producers make food by chemosynthesis.

definition.text: The total mass of living organisms in a given area or ecosystem at a particular time.

facts.text: It can be measured as wet weight, dry weight, or the mass of organic carbon, depending on the context.
In 2018 Earth's live biomass was estimated at about 550 billion tonnes of carbon, mostly in plants.
Plants hold 450 billion tonnes of carbon and bacteria plus archaea 30, while animals make up less than 0.5% of the total.
By 2020 the mass of human-made materials was projected to surpass that of all living biomass on Earth.
On land biomass falls sharply at each higher trophic level, but in the oceans it can increase at higher levels.
Ocean producers account for almost half of yearly production but only about 0.2% of total biomass.
The biomass of wild land mammals is believed to be seven times lower than prehistoric values, while livestock biomass exceeds that of all wild mammals.
